candidates.source_body_excerpt: A bomb threat at a school in Rochdale saw pupils put into lockdown this morning. St Cuthbert's Roman Catholic High School launched emergency procedures as a “precautionary measure” after a call came in this morning. School buildings were evacuated. Units from Greater Manchester Police descended on the secondary school on Shaw Road. Officers say the call was likely a hoax. Members of the public have been asked to avoid speculation on social media regarding 'false rumours' of intruders or weapons found on school grounds, Manchester Evening News reports . St Cuthbert's is expected to open again as normal on Monday. A spokesperson for St Cuthbert's Roman Catholic High School said: "Earlier this morning staff at St Cuthbert’s RC Secondary School in Rochdale received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat to the premises. "The emergency services were called and all school buildings were evacuated as a precautionary measure. All children and staff are safe and accounted for, in line with our established procedures. "Greater Manchester Police attended and parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present. "We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert’s School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority. Specialist security operatives will conduct a full sweep of the building this afternoon to confirm if any further actions are required. "Currently, the expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October - but further information will be communicated as needed when received. "Parents and carers can now attend the school to collect their children, or provide consent for their children to travel home. We’d like to thank parents, carers and colleagues for their understanding and co-operation in this matter. "We’d also urge people to avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises. More details will be communicated when appropriate, following consultation with Greater Manchester Police and the local authority." A GMP spokesperson said: "The school implemented a lockdown in response to a suspicious call. Officers attended and carried out an assessment which indicated that the call was a likely hoax. "Officers are investigating the circumstances of the call."

candidates.source_body_excerpt: More than 200 cared for children received medals during Rochdale Council's annual celebration event Young people from across the area have been celebrated for their resilience, determination, and outstanding personal progress during a special celebration event. Hundreds of medals were handed out to recognise the individual triumphs of local children who have shown incredible effort in their daily lives. Carers, teachers, and social workers submitted 273 nominations to highlight the inspiring journeys of children up to the age of 12. The awards recognised exceptional progress in school, sporting success, acts of kindness, and positive attitudes shown in the face of difficult circumstances. Youngsters enjoyed a full day of entertainment alongside their families and carers following the formal presentation ceremony. The special occasion gave local families the chance to create happy memories while celebrating the impressive achievements of the town's inspiring youth. Rochdale Borough Council hosted the annual gathering at Matthew Moss High School to ensure every nominated child received public recognition. The action-packed day featured trampolines, funfair rides, face painting, and special appearances from iconic costume characters like Spiderman. Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, said: “Nothing fills me with greater pride in my role than hearing about the tremendous achievements of our cared for children and getting the opportunity to celebrate their individual successes during Our Big Day. “They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best and this doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them. They are an absolute credit to themselves on what they have accomplished, often in the face of adversity, and they send an inspiring message to so many that no matter what life may throw at you, you will not let this stand in your way to achieve the very best for you.” A range of generous local businesses sponsored the celebration to help provide activities and entertainment for all the families attending. Business partners included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Aquatherm, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, GFM, Britania Metals, Rochdale Hornets, Axiom, The Co Op, and SRW Group.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Over two gruelling days, 18 runners will tackle sub-zero Arctic wilderness as temperatures plunge to -30°C A local fitness community in Rochdale is preparing for the ultimate test of endurance: running 100 kilometres across the freezing wilderness of Swedish Lapland to raise vital funds for four cancer charities. Starting on January 29, 2027, an 18-strong team from Resilience gym will take on the Ultra 4 Cancer challenge. Over two gruelling days, the runners will navigate sub-zero temperatures dropping as low as -30°C, pushing through deep snow with only six hours of daylight each day. The expedition is the brainchild of Resilience founder and head coach Martin Stapleton, a Rochdale-born former Royal Marines Commando and professional MMA fighter. Known for his background in elite military service and combat sports, Stapleton is no stranger to extreme fundraising, having previously kayaked the length of the Rochdale Canal and run along the River Thames to support Help for Heroes. Joining Stapleton on the trail are assistant coaches Greg Egan and Oliver Roxburgh. For Roxburgh, the cause hits particularly close to home.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans to improve the rail link between Rochdale and London have hit the buffers again. Today, the Office of Rail and Road announced it had rejected proposals for new train services which would have seen Lumo operate up to four additional return Rochdale-to-Euston services on weekdays and Saturdays and three services on Sundays . Among those backing calls for the extra services was Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, who called Lumo’s bid to restore six daily direct services between Rochdale and the capital a “game-changing opportunity” for the borough and the wider North West. But the ORR rejected the plans after its assessment found adding more trains to the West Coast Main Line — which also included services to Blackpool and Wrexham — would likely increase delays and cancelled trains for passengers. It said its assessment following detailed and extensive analysis is that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the West Coast Main Line has not materially changed since it rejected a similar application by Lumo last year. An external review commissioned by ORR also supported this conclusion. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Find out the latest events from October 17 from All Across the Arts columnist Steve Cooke Directed by Anthony Almeida, this new production of Othello aims to take a fresh look at Shakespeare’s tragedy with a greater emphasis on class differences and love. Setting the play in the 1980s around soldiers at the time of the Falklands War is a bold move that achieves some of what the director intends. Watching the performance it is striking just how clearly the issue of race, rather than class, stands out. Othello is a very successful General and Desdemona’s father, Brabantio, clearly feels that Othello, although well suited for his role as an army General, is an unsuitable match for his daughter as he is a Moor. The staging, the army uniforms and attitudes of the soldiers are effective, but for some of us with memories from the 1980s they can be somewhat unsettling. The set is stark and dark with high chicken wire fences topped by barbed wire to represent the army compound which works well for this production. The arrival of Othello himself was a moment of high theatrical drama.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: This week's column with Councillor Neil Emmott It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. candidates.source_body_excerpt: The battle for Hopwood Hall returns to the courtroom today with ownership of the historic manor house at stake. Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. The legal action initiated by Mr DePree was launched after he spent seven years working with the council to carry out vital repairs on the dilapidated site with a view to purchasing it. In November, 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with Mr DePree, and said it would explore other options because no “commercially viable” business model had been presented. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Renovating Rochdale’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks would force residents out of their homes for more than a decade, housing chiefs have said. While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Developers want to build 450 houses on former playing fields in Rochdale . The fate of one of the initial phases of the giant scheme will be decided next week. In August, Rochdale council ’s planning committee delayed making a decision on Wain Home’s plan to build 45 houses on a plot of land behind Greenvale, in Bamford. The committee felt they didn’t have enough detail about drainage from the developers. The site, to the west of Norden Road, has a history of flooding. So the panel of councillors wanted to ensure proper precautions were being taken by the developer before making a decision. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter This scheme would be the first of many for the former green belt land – which contains a number of playing fields and sports pitches. The Bamford site was taken out of green belt status after the adoption of the Greater Manchester housing strategy named Places for Everyone. A new clubhouse for Bridge FC and revamped sports pitches within the site are seen as the major benefits that would come from the overarching scheme. The plan would see access created through the demolition of Chadwick Farm Barn on Greenvale. In its place a T-junction would provide vehicle access to the site. It wasn’t just flood risks that the planning committee took issue with. Objectors at the meeting on August 5 raised concern over there being no safeguarding set in stone for how transport connectivity, drainage, highways, and local amenities would work across the whole site. To get the very latest from Manchester's political scene in your newsfeed - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source Planning agent Gareth Salthouse, representing Wain Homes, explained that drainage for the site had been assessed and said this plan could be done quickly to bring ‘much-needed housing’ to the area. The planning committee was also concerned about the lack of overall masterplan. Coun Tom Besford feared this ‘piecemeal development’ would see each developer do the bare minimum of affordable homes for each plot on the land. He felt this would eventually result in all the benefits not coming to fruition. Coun Besford said: “Why would we go through the blood, sweat and tears of getting PfE over the line but then just give this land away. We have to assume that we could get 10 other plans like this. “Then what if it doesn’t add up and everything falls short overall.” The committee agreed to defer the decision based on questions over drainage. They will reconvene on Thursday, October 22 to make a final decision on the scheme.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: People are being urged to remain vigilant following several reports of calls involving scammers impersonating police officers to obtain personal and sensitive information linked to cryptocurrency. Greater Manchester Police said one common method is to claim that they have arrested a suspect who was in possession of the victim’s personal documents, such as their passport, driving licence or banking details. On several occasions, fraudsters asked victims about their cryptocurrency accounts, specifically looking for their IDs, recovery phrases, and security codes. GMP says officers will never ask anyone to share this information or move your accounts. Police say the calls can appear convincing and are being made through spoofed GMP phone numbers. DS Reed, of GMP Cyber Crime Team, said: “These calls are an incredibly sophisticated type of crime, and those responsible are targeting our vulnerable communities. “We take offences of this nature incredibly seriously, and our team is working around the clock to understand how these offences have occurred, and how to prevent it from continuing. “Our officers will never get you to share security codes or personal information in relation to cryptocurrency, and if you are receiving calls that ask you to do so, please do not respond and report to us immediately.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A major milestone has been reached for Atom Valley with completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale, which is set to become a nationally significant gateway driving the development of the advanced materials and manufacturing cluster in the region. The 30,000 sq. ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub for advanced materials and manufacturing in Rochdale, bringing together businesses, researchers, investors and innovation partners in one location. AVID provides an environment where organisations can innovate, grow and commercialise new technologies, strengthening Greater Manchester’s position as a leading centre for advanced materials and manufacturing. Completion of the building represents a major milestone for years of partnership working between Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), The University of Manchester and wider innovation partners. RDA has led the physical development of the SMMC, working with partners to secure investment and position advanced materials and manufacturing as a priority opportunity for Rochdale and Greater Manchester. The next phase will see work move from construction towards specialist fit-out ahead of bringing the centre into operation in 2027. The RDA brought together partners from industry, academia and government to establish the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023. Since then, businesses have been able to connect with a national network of specialist expertise, facilities and innovation support through the CEAMS partners, including The University of Manchester, the Henry Royce Institute, National Physical Laboratory (NPL), Centre for Process Innovation (CPI) and NCC (formerly National Composites Centre). CEAMS has already supported more than 90 companies, developing new products and processes and demonstrating the value of a more connected innovation ecosystem.

The operation led to the execution of 20 warrants – mostly in Rochdale and Heywood – as well as in areas across Bury, Salford, Manchester, Merseyside and Yorkshire. Those arrested range in age from 19 to 49. Sixteen men have been arrested on suspicion of various offences, including drugs supply, assault, violent disorder, affray, burglary, and robbery. One woman, aged 21, was arrested on suspicion of being concerned in the supply of drugs. DS Hannah Taala, of Greater Manchester Police’s Rochdale Division, said officers focused on the crime group after violence in Heywood earlier in the year . She said: “There was a large disorder in April, where multiple people were involved in violence in the Heywood area. “It ended in some quiet serious injuries, assaults, a stab wound, using vehicles in that disorder, weapons, machetes. A cannabis farm was discovered during the raids. Image: GMP

candidates.source_body_excerpt: An album which is believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council has reached millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms. Kenion Street has enjoyed glowing reviews after being launched as part of Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture. It features local acts performing their version of a classic track originally recorded at iconic studios in the town. From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to both Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios in Kenion Street, where trailblazing artists including OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, Inspiral Carpets, Autechre, A Certain Ratio, The Fall and many others recorded some of their most memorable work. The 11 tracks on Kenion Street included PoolEra’s version of Electricity by OMD, Dreams Never End by New Order re-imagined by Medley, and Jennifer Read’s dramatic version of Totally Wired, by The Fall. Micah Stalgic and choir Local Vocals performing Atmosphere by Joy Division, that features on the album All the new tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, based in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building in Kenion Street, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. Radio 6 Music also featured the album, playing Middleton band’s K-Estate’s version of Gang of Four’s Damaged Goods. It was also made Track of the Day on Radio X with other tracks played across XS Manchester, Mersey Radio, Phoenix FM and many more, with a combined audience of over 3.5 million.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Teaching assistant Aasma Ali and husband Bilal share how opening their home changed a young girl's life forever A Rochdale couple who hesitated over fostering for nearly two years are urging others to open their homes to children in need. Teaching assistant Aasma Ali and her husband Bilal took the plunge after attending an informal lunch for foster carers. The couple were approved in just four months before welcoming an 11-year-old girl into their home. Just nine days after her arrival, the child tragically lost her birth mother, but the family pulled together to support her through the heartbreak. Two years on, the young girl has undergone an incredible transformation and grown in confidence. She has also formed a close bond with the couple's biological daughter, with the pair becoming just like real sisters. Aasma said: “I was nervous and scared. I thought the social work side of it would be too much, but my auntie, who has fostered with National Fostering Group for a long time, kept nudging me, asking why we weren't sharing our love. “Everyone at the primary school where I work kept saying the same, telling me that children need people like us. We didn't want to leave her, so we went together to do everything we could to make her feel safe. “When she first moved in, her legs were literally shaking, and she had zero confidence. Now, she has grown into a completely different girl. She has so much confidence, stands up for herself, and is figuring out who she is. "The agency helped us a lot. Whenever I have any problems, I always ring them. They bring so much knowledge and are always there for us. Just give it a go. It is like any job, if it’s not for you, you don’t have to carry on.

Terence James , 78, died after being struck by the vehicle on Shawbury Street, Middleton , on September 29, 2024. Yesterday (October 13), Manchester Crown Court heard how Ruhul Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries at the time of the offence. The 16-year-old was seen overtaking and undertaking vehicles, running red lights and weaving between lanes in the moments before the crash. Passing sentence, Judge Kate Cornell said: "The vehicle essentially became a dangerous weapon in the hands of someone unable to use it." She said Mr James would still be alive had Islam driven on the correct side of the road, telling him: "That momentary lapse of judgement caused the tragedy that everyone in this room has to deal with for the rest of their lives… None of them will ever be the same again." The court heard Islam initially tried to hide that he had been driving and instead said his older brother was behind the wheel. Investigators later found Islam and his 16-year-old friend had been making deliveries for Chilli Pot takeaway in Middleton - a business owned by family friends - at the time of the offence. Shortly after 7pm, Islam turned right from Grimshaw Lane into Shawbury Street in Middleton and struck Mr James as he crossed the road. He was on the right carriageway of the road when he was hit, having already crossed the left carriageway. Prosecuting, Philip Hall told the court Islam "cut the corner by a significant margin". Mr James suffered a serious head injury and was rushed to Salford Royal hospital, where his condition deteriorated and he never regained consciousness. His family made the heartbreaking decision to withdraw life support the following evening. A witness who was in a nearby car park on Shawbury Street heard the collision and saw Mr James lying in the road. She gave him first aid and said she was 'surprised the two Asian males were not helping', prosecutors told the court. Another witness, the court heard, saw two men get out of the Nissan Micra before running away from the car. He said one man later emerged from the nearby takeaway and repeatedly insisted his brother had been driving and was only travelling at 10mph. The court was shown dashcam footage from the vehicle in the hour before the collision, which showed the car swerving between lanes in wet weather , "aggressive" overtaking and undertaking and driving through red lights. Islam initially failed to come forward as the driver after the fatal collision, with his older brother putting himself forward instead. Families can gather to enjoy interactive art, live drumming, and the official Christmas lights launch. Visitors will journey through six interactive zones that show how the human body generates heat using mesmerising fire, light, and sound effects. Councillor Sue Smith said: “Ignite Fire Festival has become a real success story for the borough, drawing audiences from across Greater Manchester and beyond. This 2026 line-up will build on that success with new attractions, creative performances and family-friendly experiences. It will be a fantastic celebration for residents and visitors alike, setting the stage perfectly for our Christmas lights switch-on.” Bev Ayre said: “The Body is unlike anything we’ve brought to Ignite before. candidates.source_body_excerpt: National rail contractor QTS Group has hosted its first safety-focused Jamboree in Greater Manchester. The two-day event at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale brought together more than 350 colleagues, supply chain partners and activity hosts. The event was built around interactive demonstrations and hands-on activities. Attendees could see new technology and best practice from suppliers and specialists, build relationships across the supply chain, and find out more about the services available to the rail industry. Jamie Marks, HSQE Manager at QTS Group, said: “The aim of this event was to bring people together to share knowledge, strengthen relationships and highlight the importance of health, safety and innovation across our industry. “It was great to see so many colleagues and suppliers engaging with the activities and demonstrations throughout the day. The positive feedback we’ve received has been fantastic, and we’re already looking at how we can make next year’s event even bigger and better.” The QTS survey team demonstrated the Elios 3 drone and its aerial mapping capabilities. Visitors also put on virtual reality goggles for an immersive drone flight, while remote pilots flew the DJI Avata. Eurosafe provided a confined space training simulator. Attendees put on PPE and experienced conditions similar to those found in the field, while Flannery Plant Hire brought an excavator simulator for participants to test their operating skills. IRATA-trained teams ran mock aerial rescue demonstrations, and attendees could also abseil from the climbing tower on site.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Left to right: Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, with Rochdale Borough Council Leader, Councillor Neil Emmott announcing new Middleton regeneration projects. It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent 'Our Town, Our Future' event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. It is an exciting time for the town, and we are turning ambition into action. Supporting residents through the cost-of-living crisis also remains a key priority. I am proud of the help we have provided through our Helping Hand campaign, which has supported thousands of older and vulnerable residents since 2022. As global economic pressures continue to affect household finances, the council has recently approved a further package of support worth around £15 million over the next three years through the Government's Crisis and Resilience Fund. This will provide emergency financial assistance, help residents keep their homes warm, debt and welfare advice, housing support, access to food provision and free warm spaces.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Springhill Hospice is inviting nominations for its 2026 Man of Rochdale award, recognising volunteers who help others across the borough. Nominations close at midnight on Monday 2 November. Nominees must live in the borough of Rochdale, be over 18 and give their time voluntarily for the benefit of the community. They must not have already received a Royal Award such as an MBE or OBE. The winner will be announced at an awards luncheon at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 27 November. The event starts at 1pm and includes a drinks reception, three-course lunch and guest speaker. Last year’s winner was Michael Bamford, who founded Re-Use Littleborough. The non-profit organisation helps families access essential items and supports children and communities overseas. John Shaw won in 2024 after receiving more than 40 nominations for his work supporting homeless and vulnerable people. He collects and distributes food, clothing and other essentials through the Good Solution Network and local charities. Springhill Hospice says this year’s ceremony will be its 32nd. The award is sponsored by Rochdale building and construction company Jackson Jackson and Sons. Victoria Barnett, senior corporate fundraiser at Springhill Hospice, said “This is our 32nd year running the event and each year seems to get better and better. That’s all thanks to the amazing community and local heroes who help to make the event so special and demonstrate the spirit of kindness, generosity, and compassion that defines the borough.” Tickets cost £65, with tables of ten available for £650. Proceeds will support the hospice’s care for adults with terminal or life-threatening illnesses and their loved ones across Rochdale.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A school is changing the way it celebrates success and achievements following concerns about innocent images of children being turned into sexualised content. The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) and the National Crime Agency (NCA) have seen a national increase in online offenders exploiting publicly available images of children to create realistic sexual content. The IWF found 3,440 AI-generated videos of child sexual abuse in 2025, compared to just 13 in 2024, and the NCA has increasingly seen offenders using AI technologies to target children in sinister new ways. Following updated guidance from both organisations, Cardinal Langley RC High School in Middleton says it will continue to celebrate achievements of students, but will make changes to reduce the risk of altered images. In a letter to parents, deputy headteacher Angela Williams said: “The dignity and wellbeing of every young person entrusted to our care sits at the heart of our safeguarding responsibilities. Those responsibilities also require us to respond when technology changes and new risks emerge. We are therefore making an important change to the way we use photographs of pupils online. “Artificial intelligence technology has developed extremely rapidly. One consequence is that an ordinary photograph placed on a website or social-media platform can potentially be copied and used by another person to create convincing AI altered imagery. The person in the original photograph does not need to have given permission and may have no knowledge that their image has been used. Cardinal Langley will look at different ways to celebrate students’ success “Recent national safeguarding guidance for education settings has consequently encouraged schools to reconsider how identifiable images of children and young people are made publicly available online.

The centre aims to help researchers turn laboratory discoveries into commercially viable products and is expected to contribute Â£107m to the regional economy once fully operational. The Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre (SMMC), based at Kingsway Business Park next to the Metrolink stop, has been completed and will now be fitted out with specialist equipment before becoming fully operational in 2027. Scientists at the SMMC will work with colleagues at the University of Manchester, a leading centre for advanced materials research. Professor John Holden is the vice-president for civic engagement and innovation at the University of Manchester. Professor John Holden from the University of Manchester said: "We've got people inventing new materials all the time, and this facility will help scientists use those new materials in their businesses. "The scientists will be able to test how strong their new material is, how it conducts electricity and how it weathers if you leave it outside in a real-world setting."

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A major milestone has been reached for Atom Valley with completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale, which is set to become a nationally significant gateway driving the development of the advanced materials and manufacturing cluster in the region. The 30,000 sq. ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub for advanced materials and manufacturing in Rochdale, bringing together businesses, researchers, investors and innovation partners in one location. AVID provides an environment where organisations can innovate, grow and commercialise new technologies, strengthening Greater Manchester’s position as a leading centre for advanced materials and manufacturing. Completion of the building represents a major milestone for years of partnership working between Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), The University of Manchester and wider innovation partners. RDA has led the physical development of the SMMC, working with partners to secure investment and position advanced materials and manufacturing as a priority opportunity for Rochdale and Greater Manchester. The next phase will see work move from construction towards specialist fit-out ahead of bringing the centre into operation in 2027. The RDA brought together partners from industry, academia and government to establish the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023. Since then, businesses have been able to connect with a national network of specialist expertise, facilities and innovation support through the CEAMS partners, including The University of Manchester, the Henry Royce Institute, National Physical Laboratory (NPL), Centre for Process Innovation (CPI) and NCC (formerly National Composites Centre). CEAMS has already supported more than 90 companies, developing new products and processes and demonstrating the value of a more connected innovation ecosystem.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Traditional, unusual and even supernatural tales of the past will be revealed from the borough’s archives this weekend. Co-op Heritage Trust shared: “Join Mitch to uncover unusual stories and perspectives that you may never have encountered before. “These sessions promise to be creative, inspiring, and thought-provoking for everyone, whether you’re a history buff or just looking for something delightfully different to do in spooky season. “Archives are old books, documents and letters and they often don’t make it out of storage. We will be talking about folk belief, magic and the supernatural so these small group sessions are best for families with older children.” There will be hour-long drop-in sessions at 12.30pm and 2pm with no need to book.
